newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba introduces new regulations for foreign media.
newsitem.headline: Cuba introduces new regulations for foreign media.

text.p: Communist-ruled Cuba, whose own media is state-controlled, has introduced new regulations for foreign media including a stipulation that accredited foreign journalists must be "objective" in their reporting.

The regulations were signed by Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina as a ministerial resolution in February and came into force then, Cuban officials said on Tuesday. They are to be printed in a booklet and distributed soon to foreign corespondents, according to officials at the International Press Centre (CPI), the Foreign Ministry body responsible for visiting and resident foreign media in Cuba.

CPI officials, responding to questions from foreign journalists who became aware of the new rules only this week, minimised the importance of the regulations and said they did not represent a change of policy towards foreign media.

They said they were simply a compilation of norms and rules that had previously been in force for accredited foreign media representatives in Havana, currently numbering 112, and for visiting journalists.

But a group of about 30 journalists, including reporters from the main news organisations from Europe and Latin America present in Cuba, met on Monday and on Wednesday to discuss several points, particularly article 3. The group said they would send a letter of concern to authorities.

Article 3 states an accredited journalist must work "with objectivity, adhering strictly to the facts and in consonance with the professional ethics that govern journalism." Failure to do so will result in temporary or permanent withdrawal of accreditation or a "call to attention" (formal reprimand), depending on the circumstances.

CPI director Frank Gonzalez told foreign journalists on Tuesday article 3 simply put in writing what was already in practice. He said that in the last two years there had been one permanent withdrawal of an accreditation, no temporary withdrawals and several "calls to attention."
A correspondent for the Russian news agency Itar-Tass was expelled from Cuba last December after authorities said he was involved in illegal gambling.

The new regulations also stipulate that foreign journalists may work only for the news organisation for which they are accredited or must seek special permission to work for other outlets. CPI officials said this was to maintain some sort of order in news reporting out of Cuba.

This appeared to reflect the view of President Fidel Castro's government that it faces a propaganda siege from the United States and needs to be able to keep track, in particular, of news reporting to U.S. media.
Organisations such as Reuters, AFP, EFE, Notimex, Ansa, El Pais newspaper of Spain, the Financial Times of London and the British Broadcasting Corporation are present in Cuba.

Cable News Network (CNN) is the only U.S. news organisation with a permanent bureau on the island. The network opened an office in March after being granted permission by both U.S. and Cuban authorities, becoming the first U.S. news organisation with a Havana bureau in 28 years.
Washington has granted permission for nine other U.S. news organisations to come to Cuba and they have applications pending with the Cuban government.
Cuba's own media, much diminished in quantity amid economic crisis in the last six years, is defined by the constitution as in the service of a socialist society.

Small and illegal groups of dissident journalists have sprung up in recent years. They have no space in the national media but publish abroad, mostly finding an audience among the Cuban exile community in the United States.
